title: Pressure-cooker lasagna soup
subtitle: All the flavours of lasagna in a bowl, in 20 minutes
excerpt: Beef mince with tomatoes, Italian herbs, and broken lasagna sheets cooked under pressure into a rich, hearty soup. Finished with ricotta and Parmesan, a deconstructed lasagna that is faster and easier than the original.
sourceNotes: Lasagna soup is a widely shared American comfort-food adaptation that deconstructs the baked dish into a one-pot soup. The version here adds Italian-American spicing to a base that follows the ragù logic of the original.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without pasta sheets. Add broken pasta fresh when reheating. Keeps for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: Double easily and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the soup base ahead. Add pasta and cheese just before serving.

content.text: Lasagna soup takes the component parts of a classic lasagna, beef ragù, tomato, herbs, and pasta, and combines them in a soup pot. The pressure cooker produces a richly flavoured beef-and-tomato broth in about 12 minutes at pressure; broken lasagna sheets are added at the end and cook in the open pot. The finishing touch is a spoonful of ricotta and grated Parmesan in each bowl.

Break the lasagna sheets into rough 4 to 5 cm pieces, irregular shapes are part of the appeal. Add them only in the last 8 to 10 minutes of cooking in the open pot rather than under pressure, which would turn them to mush.
The ricotta is stirred through each bowl at serving. A large spoonful melts into the hot broth and creates the creamy, rich finish that distinguishes this from a simple tomato and beef soup.
Brown the mince and build the base

Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over high heat. Add the beef mince and cook, breaking it up, for 5 minutes until browned. Add the onion and garlic; cook for 3 minutes. Add the tomato puree and stir for 1 minute. Add the tinned tomatoes, {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, thyme, and bay. Season.
Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 12 minutes. Quick-release the pressure. Open the lid and discard the thyme and bay.

Bring the open pot to a brisk simmer. Add the broken lasagna sheets and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pasta is tender. Taste and adjust seasoning. Ladle into bowls and finish each with a large spoonful of ricotta and a scatter of Parmesan.

rows.symptom: The pasta sticks together in the pot
rows.cause: The pasta was not stirred regularly during the open simmer.
rows.fix: Stir every 2 minutes while the pasta cooks. The starch released from the pasta will also thicken the soup.

rows.symptom: The soup is very thick after adding pasta
rows.cause: The lasagna sheets have absorbed much of the liquid.
rows.fix: Add a splash of hot stock or water to loosen. The soup thickens quickly, serve as soon as the pasta is cooked.

content.text: Lasagna soup resolves the main objection to making lasagna on a weeknight, the layering, the béchamel, the hour in the oven. The flavour profile is the same; the method is a single pot and 30 minutes. It is particularly good for families where the appeal of lasagna is the combination of pasta, beef, and cheese rather than the specific baked format.
